lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, what is a stereotype? (An idea that everyone in a group is the same.) Today: the many parts of who you are, and belonging to groups.

Your identity is what makes you you. It includes your name, your family, the places you know and the languages you speak. It is also what you like doing, what you value, and what you are good at or learning.
Nobody is just one thing. Zara is a sister, a football fan and a good friend. She speaks Welsh and Urdu, and she builds towers. Different parts matter more at different times.
Identity grows and changes. New friends, places, skills and ideas add to it. Some parts stay, like a family story; others change, like a favourite game or a hobby.
Belonging means feeling part of a group: a family, a class, a team, a club, a faith group or a community online. Groups give support, friends and a feeling of home.

Belonging should never mean shutting others out. Good groups welcome newcomers and let people be themselves. If a group asks you to do something wrong to fit in, that is peer pressure, and you can say no.
Online, people show only part of themselves, and some pretend to be someone else. Keep your real name, school and address private, and be the same kind person online as you are face to face.
Try it in the world: build an identity tower for a game character, one layer each for a place, a skill, a language and a hobby. Next: disagreeing well.

exercises.hint: Think of all the parts of Zara.
choices: what makes you who you are
exercises.explain: Identity is all the things that make you who you are.

exercises.prompt: A person can belong to many groups at once.
exercises.hint: Think of a family, a class and a team.
exercises.explain: True: most people belong to many groups at the same time.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a group someone can belong to?
exercises.hint: A group is made of people.
exercises.explain: A sports team: its players belong to it and support each other.

choices: an idea that a whole group is the same
exercises.explain: An idea that everyone in a group is the same, which is unfair because each person is different.

exercises.hint: Think of new friends, places and skills.
exercises.explain: False: identity grows and changes as you do.

exercises.prompt: A club only lets in people who wear the same trainers. What is wrong with that?
choices: it shuts others out for no good reason
exercises.explain: It shuts people out for a reason that has nothing to do with the club.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: helps someone belong, or shuts them out?
items: inviting a new player to join
learning a friend's words in her language
exercises.explain: Helps: inviting, explaining kindly, learning a friend's words. Shuts out: teasing an accent, 'you can't sit here'.

exercises.prompt: Bram's friends say he must break a rule to stay in the group. What is this?
exercises.hint: It is pressure from people your own age.
exercises.explain: Peer pressure; Bram can say no, and a good group would not ask.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: a fixed idea about a group
exercises.hint: Which is about groups, which about you?
exercises.explain: Identity: what makes you you. Belonging: feeling part of a group. Stereotype: a fixed idea. Peer pressure: pushing you to fit in.

exercises.prompt: Online, everyone always shows their real self.
exercises.hint: Can you always tell who is behind a name?
exercises.explain: False: people show only part of themselves online, and some pretend to be someone else.

exercises.prompt: Mimi feels Scottish, Polish and a Londoner, all at once. What does this show?
exercises.hint: Can a person be several things at the same time?
choices: an identity can have many parts at once
exercises.explain: Identities have many parts, and they can all be true at once.

exercises.prompt: Which is the safest thing to show on an online game profile?
exercises.hint: Which one would not help a stranger find you?
exercises.explain: A made-up nickname; keep your real name, school and address private.

exercises.prompt: A new pupil joins who speaks little English. What would help her belong?
exercises.hint: How would you feel in a new country's school?
choices: include her and learn some of her words
exercises.explain: Including her, and learning some of her words while she learns yours, helps her feel welcome.

exercises.prompt: Belonging to a group can mean supporting each of its members.
exercises.hint: What do good groups give their members?
exercises.explain: True: good groups give support, friendship and a feeling of home.

exercises.prompt: Why do different parts of your identity matter more at different times?
exercises.hint: Think of Zara at a match, at home and at a language club.
choices: it depends on where you are and who with
it changes every hour by law
exercises.explain: Different places and people bring out different parts: a fan at a match, a sister at home.

exercises.prompt: Which part of identity often stays, and which often changes?
exercises.hint: Could it be different next year?
exercises.explain: A family story and where you were born stay; favourite games and hobbies often change.

exercises.prompt: A newcomer joins your club. Put a good welcome in order.
items: Say hello and ask their name.
Invite them into the next game.
exercises.hint: What do you do first when you meet someone new?
exercises.explain: Say hello and ask their name, show them round, then invite them into the next game.

exercises.prompt: Sort them for an online game profile: safe to share, or keep private?
exercises.hint: Could a stranger use it to find you in real life?
exercises.explain: Safe: a made-up nickname, your favourite game and a drawing. Private: your school, your address and your phone number could help a stranger find you.

exercises.prompt: Zara is many things. Match each moment to the part of her identity that matters most then.
items: chatting in Urdu with her gran
exercises.hint: Different places and people bring out different parts of who we are.
exercises.explain: At the match she is a football fan. With her gran she is an Urdu speaker. Helping her brother, she is a sister. Building, she is a builder. All of them are Zara, all at once.
